12.text: The Chukchee driver, as a rule, does not carry anything on his sledge,

13.text: for fear of fatiguing his reindeer. Even for a long journey he takes on his

14.text: sledge only a lasso, a spear, an outer coat for protection against storms, and

15.text: for provisions a cake of ground meat mixed with tallow, but no kettle and

16.text: no cup. For subsistence he depends solely on the villages and camps along

17.text: his route, or, if he fails to find these, he sleeps patiently on the snow without

18.text: meals. For the most part, however, Chukchee journeys are undertaken with

19.text: a train of from eight to ten sledges, a woman goes along to attend to it,

20.text: and a few score reindeer drag it along.

21.text: All pack-sledges have their definite place in the travelling-line, which

22.text: begins with the woman leading it, and ends with the pole-sled. One woman

23.text: can lead from ten to fifteen sledges; and a well-to-do house with a large family

24.text: may have forty or even sixty sledges, which travel in from four to six separate

25.text: lines. When starting, the sledges are packed early in the morning, and placed

26.text: in the usual order. All the lines are joined together, forming a large corral
